structure.title: Chapters 1–4 · From the castle into the army
structure.text: Candide receives lessons in the best of all possible worlds in a household where the food is good and the owner's daughter is beautiful. Outside the gate he meets recruiters with impeccable manners. What sounded like a theorem at dinner becomes a dangerous rule for judging strangers.

structure.title: Chapters 5–16 · Lisbon and the Atlantic crossings
structure.text: Earthquake, public punishment and accounts of enslavement bring quite different kinds of suffering into the same itinerary. Explanations arrive almost as regularly as disasters. The speed makes it possible to hear how rapidly a theory can dispose of pain somebody else must go on bearing.

structure.title: Chapters 17–30 · Eldorado and the price of getting home
structure.text: In a place where the streets abound in precious stones, the travellers spot a chance to be rich somewhere else. Once they leave, the problem of transporting their wealth and finding the people they want puts a surprisingly material strain on philosophical optimism.

people.name: Pangloss
people.text: His great gift is the phrase that explains an event after it has happened. Even when events cost him dearly he can remain faithful to his system. The comedy sharpens whenever Candide needs practical assistance.

people.name: Cunégonde and the old woman
people.role: Travellers with histories of their own
people.text: When either woman gets the floor, an adventure the men might describe in a sentence becomes a history of hazards borne by a particular body. The old woman's tale even puts competing claims to have suffered most into comic dispute.

context.title: What Pangloss has to prove
context.text: Calling this the best possible world allows for individual horrors provided each belongs to the best arrangement of the whole. Voltaire keeps putting the speaker who knows how the whole works in front of the person paying the local bill.

notice.text: Notice the narrator's courtesy during a catastrophe.
notice.why: An execution or a battle can receive the polished treatment of a ceremony. The elegance gives the reader a moment to hear the institutions congratulating themselves while the bodies accumulate.

notice.text: Look at the people who offer transport, food or shelter.
notice.why: Often the question of whether somebody gets through the night depends on a stranger willing to share something. Voltaire can give the decisive act in a chapter to someone with no system to expound.

opening: Candide has been taught that he lives in the best of all possible worlds. Expelled from the house where he grew up, he encounters war, persecution, and an earthquake, while the philosophy meant to explain his good fortune proves equally capable of explaining everybody’s suffering. Voltaire sends this earnest pupil through one disaster after another in a comedy whose cruelty falls as much on the explanations as on the victims. Candide keeps trying to believe what experience makes increasingly difficult to defend.
